opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few gaps, and the biggest one, at least from where I sit, is learning from experience.

Today's models are extremely good at absorbing what humans have already written down. Pre-training compresses a huge amount of human knowledge, and post-training, including RL, shapes how the model uses that knowledge. But a lot of the model's ability is still borrowed from human data. A human, or even an animal, can go into a new environment, try things, fail, and actually update themselves from that experience in a lasting way. Our models mostly can't do that yet. Once deployment starts, the weights are basically frozen. The model can do some in-context adaptation, but when the context window ends, that's gone.

The second gap is long-horizon work. If you give a model a task that takes a few minutes, it's often superhuman. If you give it a task that takes a few weeks, where it has to plan, keep track of what it's done, notice it went down the wrong path, and recover, it falls apart much more often. A lot of real intelligence is about reliability over long horizons, not peak performance on one question.

The third is the environment and reward problem, which is very close to my own work in RL. RL works really well when you have a clear signal: did the code pass the tests, did you solve the math problem. But most of what we care about in the real world doesn't come with a clean reward. Building rich enough environments and good enough feedback, so the model can keep improving on open-ended tasks, is still an unsolved infrastructure and research problem.

So I'd say the models are already very knowledgeable, and in narrow ways very smart. What's missing is the loop where an agent acts in the world, gets feedback, and keeps getting better on its own. When that loop really works at scale, I think that's when people will start feeling like it's AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a big question, and I think the honest answer is that we've gotten really good at one thing and mistaken it for the whole thing.

What current models do extremely well is pattern completion over an enormous amount of human-generated data. Give them a problem that looks like problems people have written about, and they'll produce something that looks like a good answer, often one that actually is a good answer. That's genuinely impressive, and I don't want to downplay it. But when you push on it, you find the edges pretty fast.

The first edge is continual learning. If I work with a person for a month, they get better at working with me. They remember what went wrong last Tuesday, they adjust. A model today is frozen the moment training ends. Everything it "learns" during a conversation evaporates when the context closes. We paper over that with longer context windows and retrieval tricks, but that's not the same as actually updating your understanding of the world from experience. Humans do that constantly and cheaply. We don't have a clean way to do it yet.

The second edge is reliability on long-horizon tasks. Models can do a single step well, but when you chain a hundred steps together, small errors compound. A person who's competent at something can notice they're drifting off course and correct. Models are getting better at this, especially with reinforcement learning on agentic tasks, but the failure modes are still weird. They'll be brilliant for forty steps and then do something no competent intern would ever do. That brittleness tells me the underlying representation isn't the same kind of thing as human understanding, even when the outputs look similar.

The third thing, and this is more my own view, is that we've mostly been measuring progress on benchmarks that reward exactly what these systems are good at. Exams, coding problems, puzzles with known answers. Those are the easiest things to generate training signal for. The things that matter for general intelligence, like figuring out what the right question even is, or operating in a messy environment where the reward isn't given to you, are much harder to measure, so they get less optimization pressure. I think we're a bit ahead of where we actually are because our rulers are biased.

So when people ask me if we're close, I say: we're close on the axis we've been pushing on, and surprisingly far on a couple of axes we haven't figured out how to push on yet. The gap isn't scale. It's that a few core capabilities, learning from experience and acting robustly over time, don't just fall out of predicting the next token, at least not with the setups we have now.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the difficulty is that we don’t have a clear, shared definition of AGI. If we mean a system that can perform well on many different tasks, current AI already shows impressive breadth. But if we mean a system that can reliably handle unfamiliar situations, learn from experience, and pursue a goal without constant human guidance, there are still substantial gaps.

For me, the distinction is between producing a convincing answer and having an understanding that remains reliable when the situation changes. A model can explain a principle very well and then fail to apply it in a slightly different context. That suggests that strong performance alone doesn’t establish general intelligence.

So I wouldn’t say there is necessarily one missing ingredient. It may require progress in reasoning, memory, learning, and interaction with the world—and making those capabilities work together reliably. The question is whether a system can adapt when the task is unfamiliar and nobody is there to tell it what to do next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the difficulty is that we don’t have a universally agreed definition of AGI. Today’s models are very capable at language and many other tasks, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they can learn and act reliably in an unfamiliar environment.

They can solve a difficult problem and then fail on a simple variation. They also struggle with long-term planning, learning continuously from experience, and knowing when their own answers are wrong. Those abilities matter if we want a system that can operate independently beyond the situations it was trained for.

So I wouldn’t say there’s one missing ingredient. The question is whether scaling our current methods will resolve those weaknesses, or whether we need additional approaches to learning, memory, and interaction with the world. I think that’s still open.
